newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan warlord faces Taleban, wants peace.
newsitem.headline: Afghan warlord faces Taleban, wants peace.

text.p: Forces of Afghan warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum, armed with tanks, guns and missiles, maintained a tense stand-off with Kabul's new Taleban masters on Wednesday at a vital tunnel northwest of the capital.
However both the northern Uzbek leader's faction, and the Islamic Taleban militia now in control of Kabul, appeared keen to avoid a confrontation at the Salang tunnel and no fighting was reported.

Colonel-General Chary, commander of Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli frontline position, told reporters in what had the ring of a warning to the Taleban forces: "We don't want to fight but we will defend our territory."

Chary, speaking at his position overlooking the village of Olang, said Taleban forces were about three km (two miles) to the south. "We command the heights -- there has been no fighting here," he said.
He had well-armed positions, including multiple-launch Grad missiles, tanks and heavy artillery, at both ends of the strategically vital tunnel, around 70 km (45 miles) from Kabul.
Taleban Acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammed Stanakzai told reporters on Tuesday their forces did not want to fight Dostum.
The Taleban, who seized Kabul last Friday with barely a shot fired, are focusing on a perceived threat from former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
Dostum's representative in Moscow, Aref Shakhra, confirmed that the general hoped to avoid conflict.
"What (Dostum) wants for Afghanistan is peace. He does not want to fight," Shakhra told Reuters, adding that Dostum would be interested in taking part in a new Taleban-led government.
"But if someone attacks him he has the means to defend himself without foreign aid," he said.

Russia's new national security chief, Alexander Lebed, suggested on Tuesday that Russia and other ex-Soviet republics might provide "material and moral" support to Dostum, Massoud and Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar.
Dostum's representative in Moscow said there had so far been no concrete offers of help from the Russian authorities.
The comments by Lebed, who once served with the Soviet Red Army in Afghanistan, drew a sour response from another Russian veteran of the Afghan conflict, General Boris Gromov.
"When they say they want to help the adversaries of the Taleban, Russian politicians would do better to find out about the possibilities of their own country," Gromov told Interfax news agency.
Russia "has not the material or military means" to help the Afghans, said Gromov, who helped oversee the Soviet military withdrawal from the central Asian country in the late 1980s.

Taleban-controlled Kabul Radio said on Wednesday their forces had entered the Panjsher Valley, Masood's stronghold, but said the front-line near the Salang tunnel between Taleban troops and those of Dostum was quiet.

The Taleban on Tuesday disowned an ultimatum sent by a Taleban commander to Dostum's forces the previous day which had told them to stand aside and let the Taleban cross the Salang pass over the formidable Hindu Kush mountain range.
"So far, we have no problem with Dostum and we hope this will be solved through negotiations. We don't want more fighting," the Taleban's Stanakzai said.
Military experts said on Tuesday that Masood and Dostum might have to bury an old rivalry to confront the Taleban.
Dostum, a former defence minister, was involved in an attempt to seize Kabul in a military coup on January 1, 1994, setting off bloody fighting with Masood forces.
Aides to Masood at a secret location in the Panjsher Valley said on Tuesday that some contacts were continuing with Dostum, but indicated that the two men were far from reaching an agreement.
